content.question: On whose recommendation were Fundamental Duties included in the Indian Constitution?
content.note:
The Swaran Singh Committee was set up by the Government of India in 1976 to make recommendations about fundamental duties.
Based on its report, the 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act was passed.
Note: Initially, the committee suggested 8 duties, but the government included 10. Other options: Committees like Verma Committee (1999) later looked into the legal provisions for enforcing these duties.

content.question: From which country was the concept of Directive Principles of State Policy taken?
content.note:
The Directive Principles of State Policy (DPSP) were borrowed from the Constitution of Ireland (which had itself copied it from the Spanish Constitution).
These principles are listed in Part IV (Articles 36-51) and serve as guidelines for the government. Related info: While DPSPs are non-justiciable (cannot be enforced in court), they are fundamental in the governance of the country.

content.question: Which article of the Indian Constitution abolishes the concept of Untouchability?
content.note:
Article 17 of the Indian Constitution states that 'Untouchability' is abolished and its practice in any form is forbidden.
It is a Fundamental Right aimed at promoting social equality.
Note: The enforcement of any disability arising out of 'Untouchability' is an offense punishable in accordance with law under the Protection of Civil Rights Act, 1955.

content.question: When were the initial 10 fundamental duties included in the Constitution?
content.note:
The initial 10 Fundamental Duties were included in the Constitution in 1976.
This was done through the 42nd Amendment Act during the Emergency. Related info: These duties were added to a new part, Part IV-A, under a single Article, 51A. The 11th duty was added much later in 2002.

content.question: Which words were added to the Preamble by the 42nd Amendment (1976)?
content.note:
The 42nd Amendment (1976) added three specific words to the Preamble: Socialist, Secular, and Integrity.
This amendment is often called the 'Mini-Constitution' because of the massive changes it brought.
Note: This remains the only time the Preamble of India has been amended to date.

content.question: Which Amendment abolished the right to property as a fundamental right in 1978?
content.note:
The 44th Amendment Act (1978) removed the Right to Property from the list of Fundamental Rights.
It was formerly under Article 19(1)(f) and Article 31. Current Status: It is now a Legal Right under Article 300A in Part XII. The amendment was brought by the Janta Government to rectify excesses of the 42nd Amendment.

content.question: Which article gives Parliament the power to amend its provisions?
content.note:
Article 368 in Part XX of the Constitution deals with the powers of Parliament to amend the Constitution and its procedure.
It ensures the Constitution is a 'living document'. Important Note: According to the Kesavananda Bharati case (1973), Parliament cannot amend the 'Basic Structure' of the Constitution.

content.question: How many fundamental duties are prescribed in Part IV A (Article 51A)?
content.note:
There are currently 11 Fundamental Duties listed in Article 51A.
Originally there were 10; the 11th (providing education opportunities to children) was added by the 86th Amendment Act, 2002.
Note: Fundamental Duties are inspired by the Constitution of the erstwhile USSR.

content.question: Which Amendment Act, 2002 provides free and compulsory primary education as a right?
content.note:
The 86th Amendment Act, 2002 inserted Article 21A to provide free and compulsory education to all children between 6 and 14 years.
It made Right to Education a Fundamental Right. Related info: This amendment also changed the subject matter of Article 45 in DPSP and added the 11th Fundamental Duty.

content.question: What is the tenure of the Chief Election Commissioner of India?
content.answer: 6 years or until the age of 65, whichever is earlier.
content.note:
The Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) holds office for a term of 6 years or until the age of 65 years, whichever is earlier.
This ensures the independence and stability of the Election Commission.
Note: The CEC has a status and salary equal to that of a Judge of the Supreme Court of India.

content.question: Who presides over the joint sitting of both Houses of Parliament in case of a deadlock?
content.note:
The Speaker of the Lok Sabha presides over the joint sitting of both Houses.
In the absence of the Speaker, the Deputy Speaker of Lok Sabha presides. Important Note: The Chairman of Rajya Sabha never presides over a joint sitting because he/she is not a member of either House. The Deputy Chairman of Rajya Sabha may preside if the Speaker and Deputy Speaker are absent.

content.question: Which article relates to the organization of Gram Panchayats?
content.note:
Article 40 directs the State to organize Village Panchayats and endow them with such powers and authority as may be necessary.
It is a Gandhian Principle under the Directive Principles of State Policy. Related info: This was later given constitutional status via the 73rd Amendment Act.

content.question: Who summons the joint sitting of both Houses of the Indian Parliament?
content.note:
The President of India has the power to summon a joint sitting of both Houses under Article 108.
A joint sitting is called to resolve a deadlock between the Lok Sabha and the Rajya Sabha over the passage of an Ordinary Bill.
Note: A joint sitting cannot be called for a Money Bill or a Constitutional Amendment Bill.

content.question: If the Prime Minister submits his resignation to the President, what does it mean?
content.answer: Resignation of the entire Council of Ministers
content.note:
The resignation of the Prime Minister means the resignation of the entire Council of Ministers.
The PM is the keystone of the cabinet arch; the Council of Ministers cannot exist without the PM.
Note: This is based on the principle of Collective Responsibility where the ministry sinks or swims together.

content.question: What does the Indian Constitution describe India as?
content.note:
Article 1 of the Constitution describes India, that is Bharat, as a 'Union of States'.
This signifies that the Indian federation is not the result of an agreement by the states (like the USA) and states have no right to secede from the union.
Note: It emphasizes the indestructible nature of the Union.

content.question: What is the source of authority of the Indian Constitution?
content.note:
The People of India are the ultimate source of authority.
The Preamble begins with the words, "We, the People of India...", indicating that the Constitution derives its power directly from the citizens. Related info: This establishes the principle of Popular Sovereignty.

content.question: Which constitutional amendment reduced the voting age from 21 to 18?
content.note:
The 61st Amendment Act, 1988 reduced the voting age from 21 to 18 years for the Lok Sabha and State Legislative Assembly elections.
It was intended to encourage youth participation in the democratic process.
Note: This amendment modified Article 326 of the Constitution.

content.question: Who is also known as the first/main legal officer of the Government of India?
content.note:
The Attorney General of India is the highest law officer in the country.
Appointed by the President under Article 76, they give advice to the Government of India upon legal matters. Unique Power: The Attorney General has the right to speak and take part in the proceedings of both Houses of Parliament but cannot vote.

content.question: Which article abolishes the concept of titles?
content.note:
Article 18 abolishes titles and prohibits the state from conferring any titles other than military or academic distinctions.
It ensures social equality by preventing the state from creating a class of privileged citizens.
Note: National awards like Bharat Ratna and Padma awards are not considered 'titles' in this context.

content.question: What does Article 32 of the Indian Constitution relate to?
content.note:
Article 32 provides the Right to Constitutional Remedies, which allows citizens to move the Supreme Court for the enforcement of Fundamental Rights.
It gives the court power to issue Writs. Significance: Without this article, all other fundamental rights would be meaningless as there would be no way to protect them.

content.question: Out of 245 members of the Rajya Sabha, how many members are nominated by the President?
content.note:
The President nominates 12 members to the Rajya Sabha.
These members are chosen from people having special knowledge or practical experience in Literature, Science, Art, and Social Service.
Note: The remaining members are elected representatives of the States and Union Territories.

content.question: Which set of articles relates to emergency provisions?
content.note:
Articles 352 to 360 in Part XVIII deal with emergency provisions.
352 (National Emergency), 356 (President's Rule), and 360 (Financial Emergency).
Note: During an emergency, the federal structure of India turns into a Unitary one without a formal amendment.

content.question: Under Article 312, what special power does the Rajya Sabha possess?
content.answer: The power to create new All India Services
content.note:
Under Article 312, the Rajya Sabha can pass a resolution (supported by not less than two-thirds of members present and voting) to create one or more All India Services.
This is a special federal power of the Rajya Sabha to protect the interests of the states. Example: The Indian Forest Service was created this way in 1966.

content.question: Which article mentions Uniform Civil Code?
content.note:
Article 44 (a Directive Principle) states that the State shall endeavor to secure for the citizens a Uniform Civil Code (UCC) throughout the territory of India.
It aims to replace personal laws based on religion with a common set of laws for every citizen. Current Status: Currently, Goa is the only Indian state with a UCC.

content.question: Who administers the oath of office to the Vice President of India?
content.note:
The President of India (or some person appointed by him) administers the oath of office to the Vice President.
According to Article 69, the Vice President must make and subscribe an oath before entering office.
Note: The Vice President is the Ex-officio Chairman of the Rajya Sabha.

content.question: Which article relates to the Attorney General of India?
content.note:
Article 76 provides for the office of the Attorney General for India.
He is the Chief Legal Advisor to the Government. Term: He holds office during the pleasure of the President, meaning there is no fixed tenure mentioned in the Constitution.

content.question: The provision for Constitutional Amendment Proposals is borrowed from which country?
content.note:
The procedure for the amendment of the Constitution was borrowed from South Africa.
This includes the method of passing amendment bills by a special majority.
Note: The provision for the election of members of Rajya Sabha was also borrowed from South Africa.

content.question: For the protection of fundamental rights, how many types of writs can be issued by the Supreme Court?
content.note:
The Supreme Court can issue five types of writs: Habeas Corpus, Mandamus, Prohibition, Certiorari, and Quo-Warranto.
These are tools to protect the Fundamental Rights of citizens under Article 32.
Note: High Courts also have this power under Article 226, which is actually broader than the Supreme Court's power.

content.question: Which Act abolished the system of Dyarchy at the provincial level?
content.note:
The Government of India Act, 1935 abolished 'Dyarchy' (dual government) in the provinces and introduced 'Provincial Autonomy'.
However, it introduced Dyarchy at the Centre. Related info: This Act served as the main blueprint for the current Indian Constitution.

content.question: Which article states that all executive actions shall be taken in the name of the President?
content.note:
Article 77 states that all executive actions of the Government of India shall be expressed to be taken in the name of the President.
Even though the PM is the real head, the President is the formal/titular head of the state.
Note: The President makes rules for the more convenient transaction of government business.
